idiom_name: abstract service interface + constructor-injected gateways, RAII transaction guard
implementation_notes: The classic form is written by hand: an abstract interface per subject area, a concrete service class taking its gateways by constructor (or template parameter), and a transaction guard that begins in its constructor and commits explicitly or rolls back in its destructor - RAII, as the standard library does for mutexes and pointers. C++ offers no dependency-injection container and no transaction manager, so the wiring lives in the composition root (main or a bootstrap module) and substitutability is either virtual dispatch (runtime) or template policies (compile time, no virtual call). The structure is still justified when several front ends share the operations; a single application can usually call the gateways directly.
pitfalls: A transaction guard's destructor must not throw, so rollback failures are silently dropped - log the failure instead of terminating.
Services hold references to their gateways: a service that outlives the composition root's gateways is a dangling-reference bug, not a compile error.
If the service is only ever instantiated with one concrete combination, template parameters remove the per-operation virtual call; keeping virtual dispatch 'for flexibility' costs in hot paths.
